title: How to measure if AI agents actually use your Design System
description: What I learned from Christoph Hellmuth at our AI Jam on September 29 2026 Christoph Hellmuth is Design Engineering Manager for Design Systems at NordVPN . His team builds Aurora. That is the design system behind NordVPN and other Nord Security products. At our AI Jam he showed Open Design System Bench . It is an open source tool that measures how well AI agents follow your design system and gives you a score from 0 to 100. These are my notes from his session. 😱 The AGENTS.md was there and the models still built their own buttons Christoph’s team did what everyone recommends. Aurora ships an AGENTS.md. Then they measured what the models actually did with it. In 41 of 57 guided generations the models hand-rolled buttons, dialogs and toggles instead of using the design system they were told about. That is 72%. “It just invented a button, and honestly, we were quite shocked, because we were thinking, like, yeah, best practices, they work well.” Every model launch comes with a scoreboard like SWE-bench or Terminal-Bench. None of them checks whether an agent uses your Button instead of inventing one. That gap hurts when leadership asks what the 50 to 80 hours of AI readiness work brought. Without a number you only have a feeling. “Cool, so can you prove it? And you… well, we did all these best practices, but not really, and that’s not really what leadership wants to hear.” 🔍 Two tools: a free audit and a behavioral benchmark The static audit reads your repo. It costs nothing and took 5 to 10 seconds in Christoph’s live demo. It checks what you ship for agents such as AGENTS.md, llms.txt, skills and catalog quality. You get a score plus a list of what is missing. The behavioral benchmark lets an agent build real screens with your system in a fresh workspace. Then it grades the result. You can also run the audit against several systems at once. Christoph compared open source systems like Carbon, Primer, Base UI and MUI. Chakra scored highest with 70.5. “In this just static check of 10 seconds, it also gives you basically a to-do list, and you can now go into Jira, create the tickets for the next month.” The audit score is always the optimistic one. Ticking checkboxes is easy. The real score shows up once an agent has to use your system. 📝 Tasks describe intent and never the component The benchmark ships with 10 tasks. One example is a password reset screen. Another is the area where a user cancels a subscription. A task never names a component. Otherwise you only test whether the model can read. You can write your own tasks and weigh the rubric yourself. Christoph’s example: a red destructive cancel button can count for more than a support link. A built-in linter checks your task before you run it. In his demo it failed a task because the prompt mentioned the real export PasswordInput . 📊 What gets graded Each output is scored on six dimensions. The weights come from the README : imports (10%): Only your package, React and local files are imported apiFidelity (25%): No hallucinated components or invented props tokenDiscipline (15%): No raw hex values, arbitrary Tailwind or hardcoded styles a11yStatic (10%): Accessible names, labels and valid ARIA compile (10%): TypeScript compiles judgment (30%): Per-task rubric graded by a separate model By default every task runs 3 times per model. The worst run counts so the score never looks better than what a designer would get on a bad day. The hallucinations Christoph found in Aurora were very specific. Aurora has a heading prop and the model invented a Heading component. Aurora has Text and the model used Typography . It also invented spacing props on Box and Card. “They hand over the AI generated prototype to developers. And they tell you, well, we don’t really have any of these props, or this is an invented component.” 📉 The repo read 20 points better than it behaved Christoph ran the benchmark on Aurora AppKit. The audit gave it 64.8. Six models building with it scored 44.9. Only 10 of 55 guided cells compiled against the published types. The npm run produced about 250 type errors. About 100 of them came from direction="column" on a prop that only takes 'vertical' | 'horizontal' . The uncomfortable part: their own AGENTS.md and DESIGN.md mentioned a cn helper and a bare Radix component that never existed in the codebase. Their docs were teaching the agent some of the traps. 💡 One sentence in the README flipped it Their AGENTS.md told the model what not to use. In the run against the source code 72% of the buttons were still hand-rolled. Then they added one sentence to the README saying the package is installed. In the run against the npm package only 22% were hand-rolled. “Even things you thought, oh, this is useless, like, why should I tell the AI that my design system package is installed? No, it actually makes a difference.” After fixing the findings the audit score went from 64.8 to 82.0. The fixes included exporting the types nobody had exported and generating an llms.txt. He also tested six open models with and without an AGENTS.md. In the session he said adding one file moved the scores by 20 to 30 points. His write-up lists DeepSeek V4 Pro going from 58.7 to 84.8 and Sonnet 5 single-shot going from 51.2 to 75.3. 🛠️ How to run it on your design system The repo supports React and TypeScript libraries plus web components built with Stencil or Lit. Your system can be local source or an npm package. Clone open-design-system-bench Install and set it up: npm install npx tsx src/cli.ts init # wizard asks for package name, location and how you serve it npx tsx src/cli.ts doctor # checks your config and CLI setup npx tsx src/cli.ts extract # builds the component catalog npx tsx src/cli.ts run --profile smoke # 2 cells in about 5 minutes Run the bigger profiles once the smoke test passes. small has 5 cells for weekly checks and full has 90 cells for a quarterly baseline. You do not have to type any of this. Christoph and I both said it in the session: paste the repo link into Claude Code and ask it to install the benchmark and run it against your design system. A full run with Claude Code took him half an hour to an hour. His run with 6 models took about 3 hours. Watch the cost. Through the API a run with the top models can cost a few hundred dollars. A subscription is much cheaper. Christoph’s tip for the report: give it to Claude and ask for a PDF for leadership with an executive summary, the models tested, the results and the costs. 🎨 What about Figma? Vee asked in the Q&A whether you can score Figma and code together. Christoph’s answer: a Figma file alone mostly tests how well the AI uses the Figma MCP. It says little about your design system. His recommendation for the Figma to code workflow is Code Connect. “Honestly, at least from what we’ve seen, CodeConnect is totally worth having for, your Figma to code, workflow.” What I’m taking back to my own work These are my own takeaways and not Christoph’s: Run the free audit first. It takes seconds and gives you a ticket list. Never trust the audit score alone. Aurora lost 20 points once agents had to build with it. Tell the agent what to use and not only what to avoid. Grep your own AGENTS.md for helpers and components that do not exist. Write benchmark tasks the way a designer would brief a screen. Never name the component. title: Out There
description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! “Writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Fall (or at least post-summer) finally seems to be arriving here in New Orleans. And it is almost time — wherever you are — for Write Out . This is an annual undertaking of the National Writing Project , developed in conjunction with the National Park Service . As I wrote last year : The core idea is pretty simple: get outside, and write. Write about your environment, write to your environment, observe and attend to nature, use the craft of writing to sharpen your senses, and use your senses to sharpen your writing. “The goal is to be inspired by the world around us ,” the NWP writes, “and to connect and learn through place-based writing and sharing.” Nothing (well, maybe apart from the actual weather) is stopping you from writing outside any time. But Write Out is a kick in the pants, a kind of open-to-anyone annual two-week event, which the NWP promotes through various prompts and other resources aimed at educators but available to all. This year Write Out happens October 11–25, with the lovely theme Write Where We Stand — “writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Every year NWP publishes a “ choice board ” of theme-related prompts; here are a few (condensed and slightly modified versions) of my favorites for this year. (Click through on each prompt title for the full NWP context/instructions.) Poetically Advocate A Place You Love . Take inspiration from Don Welch’s poem “ Advice From a Provincial ,“ and identify three “outdoor images or phenomena that are wondrous about your place. Use them to create a poetic letter to someone who doesn’t really know” the place you love, or at least not like you know it. Link Words and Image s. Snap some pictures around your community. Take your time. Choose one that captures something to celebrate — and one that captures something you would like to change. Pair these images. “ What story do they tell when you look at them together? Give your story a title, caption your images, and share your work.” Speak Like A River. Poets Amanda Eke and Mario José Pagán Morales consider the Bronx River, and what stories it might tell. In a place you know, reflect on “ what that place has witnessed , remembered, celebrated, protected, or survived. … If this river, tree, park, or wooded pathway could talk — tell us poems, tell us stories — what do you think it would say?” Write about it. Leave a comment THERE’S MORE! In connection with Write Out, there are two online events that sound cool: Hawaiian Kilo: Writing Rooted in Place Native Hawaiians developed a practice known as Kilo — “to watch, observe, examine, or forecast.” This means closely observing the natural world and its patterns, ideally to better steward the environment. A Zoom workshop, “led by teachers from the Waiākea Intermediate School in Hilo Hawai'i,” happens October 13, 2026, 6 pm US Central time . Details and (free) registration here . Haiku + Comic = Haikomic The Write Time with Write Out Ambassador Grant Snider on October 20 . Snider is a writer/artist who combines haiku with comics. (Details on that here , and at his newsletter. ) And he is this year’s Write Out Author Ambassador. Check the Write Out newsletter for event details as they emerge. I really like the sound of this and hope to revisit. Grant Snider, via Incidental Comics Leave a comment PS I was a Write Out Ambassador last year. I love Write Out! title: Looking and Learning
description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! Nathan Cima via Unsplash “Look out into the world and notice not in the way you want to, but in the way the world needs you to.” Recently I enjoyed an interesting email exchange and conversation with Dr. Brett Criswell, an associate professor of Secondary Education at West Chester University in West Chester, Pennsylvania. In short, Brett teaches people how to be teachers . And as it happens, he has a specific interest of the role that attention and noticing play in crafting an optimal classroom experience. In our exchanges, Brett introduced me to the idea of “professional vision.” That is explained further below, but basically refers to the way members of different professions will be conditioned to notice particular things in particular ways. So for example a teacher and a police officer might notice different details of the same scenario. That job-specific attention skill is important: a teacher may need, for instance, to notice students’ body language, in addition to what they’re saying. But lately, Brett’s work is also exploring what he calls a more “humanistic” approach to attention, and turns out (I’m excited to say) that TAoN has been a resource! So I decided to ask him some questions, to see what the TAoN community and I can learn. Here goes! TAoN: You mentioned a 1994 paper by Charles Goodwin (an anthropologist) about “professional vision.” What does that mean? Brett Criswell : Most people treat vision — and the attention that directs it — as a trait in the head of an individual. But Goodwin made a strong case for the fact that attention is very much social , especially when it comes to our work within professions. Each profession trains people coming into that profession in relation to what to pay attention to in the settings in which they do work — something that Goodwin labeled highlighting . I spend a lot of time as a teacher educator trying to help my pre-service teachers learn how to pay attention, in the buzz and chaos that is a typical classroom, to what is truly crucial to student learning. Being a “teacher educator” means you teach people to be teachers, as it were. Recently you and some colleagues published research in a journal called The New Educator in which you proposed “new lens on noticing — a humanistic one.” What does that mean? What form does it potentially take? The issue that we tried to make visible in that article is that many people that study attention in education treat it as an individual action based on our psychology. So, they are focused on getting individuals better at paying attention to what they think individuals should be paying attention to (in education). My previous answer above shows that I care about that, too. But I also care about how noticing more meaningfully can help enrich our lives and provide us with a pathway to wellbeing. That’s why I was drawn to The Art of Noticing , and why I mentioned it in The New Educator article: Noticing in the most productive way possible allows us to self-actualize and even self-transcend — become the best, most content versions of ourselves and then eventually move past our own needs. What’s the potential advantage to this approach? I mean obviously I’m in the camp that being attentive and engaged is a better way to live in general! But is there a case to be made that it might benefit or complement “professional vision”? First, yes to your notion that being attentive and engaged is a better way to live in general. But I think it can go beyond that. Iris Murdoch wrote about the morality of attention — that centering attention on others rather than ourselves make us better, both for ourselves and for others. I think if we can develop professional vision in pre-service teachers in a way that aligns with Murdoch’s philosophy, they will not only be better at noticing what they need to in the classroom, they will better serve the students with whom they work — and, in the end, themselves. How have you experimented in your classes with the “humanistic” approach? One thing I do in an introductory education course is provide eight different strategies drawn from TAoN . I ask my students to try at least one of them, and then to share their experience on a discussion board, and to read and respond to each other’s posts. In class, I highlight the posts that I think support a humanistic approach — like when, for instance, students describe how engaging in the activities caused them to take on new perspectives or to see familiar things in a different way. Those shifts I think are a starting point to tapping into the power of noticing to promote a humanistic stance on this capacity. But, I still have work to do fully realizing the potential of this approach. Anything I should have asked? And of course we’d love a prompt or two! I think the last thing we all need to consider is how we do this — how do we notice the world in ways that allow us to “suck the marrow” out of life, as Thoreau implored? Two particular ideas about the how are unselfing (an idea from Murdoch) and negation (from the Order of the Third Bird ). I present the notion of unselfing to my students this way: “ Look out into the world and notice not in the way you want to, but in the way the world needs you to .” The idea of negation comes from the approach the Order, a group dedicated to noticing the world fully, uses: They notice an object, then walk away from it for some period of time to get rid of their initial impressions ; then they go back and re-notice it. There’s more on that Third Bird exercise here: My thanks to Brett Criswell! I hope this is the beginning of a discussion, not an end. Brett also told me that a couple of his colleagues are conducting a workshop and research program involving “self-awareness and noticing strategies within [the] professional setting.” I’ll let you know if anything notable comes of it, it sounds really interesting. Meanwhile, what do you think? I’m particularly curious to hear thoughts from the educators out there, but really all perspectives (and questions) welcome! title: #307 | Cronicamente offline
description: nas edições anteriores #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2) #306 | Uma seleção de campanhas tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 “A habilidade mais importante do próximo século não vai ser conectar humanos com mais tecnologia. Vai ser conectar humanos uns com os outros”. _ “Ninguém confia no gosto de quem só consome fast-food”. _ Em 2025, a WGSN já tinha previsto que a fadiga digital e o excesso de estímulos levaria as pessoas a migrarem para comunidades no mundo real: “Até 2027, a busca por menos barulho e mais desconexão digital vai ser o novo normal, emergindo como uma demonstração de autocuidado em forma de ambientes mais calmos, seguros e significativos” Isso tem se traduzido na realização e/ou incentivo de todo tipo de experiência. Um grande destaque no Brasil, que ilustra tanto o pertencimento quanto o autocuidado e, claro, a presença das marcas, são as corridas de rua. Segundo a Exame , em 2024 foram realizadas 2.827 corridas de rua oficiais no país. Em 2025, mais de 5 mil. Além disso, temos visto o crescimento de eventos em lojas, jantares especiais para clientes, clubes do livro, exibições em salas de cinema e convites para as mais diversas atividades físicas, manuais, intelectuais e sociais. E assim seguirá essa tendência - em 2027 e além. O que nos traz à edição de hoje é a sua relação com a creator economy . No que o Digiday chamou de “ vibes over metrics ”, os eventos presenciais agora são também uma estratégia de engajamento e construção de comunidade para marcas pessoais - ou marcas essencialmente virtuais. _ Três movimentos estão por trás disso: 1 - O mundo “pós-feed”, em que as redes sociais se tornaram oficialmente plataformas de descoberta e entretenimento, e onde “número de seguidores” é uma métrica cada vez menos determinante de sucesso e engajamento. Hoje, a viralização está muito mais ligada à adequação de um conteúdo a um nicho, assunto, tom ou formato (ou todos ao mesmo tempo). Mas quando encontrar uma audiência tem se tornado mais fácil, aprofundar essa relação é o desafio. Seja criando um universo de marca que gere reconhecimento e lembrança, seja reunindo essas pessoas para além do feed. 2 - A busca por mais presença , que é comum a todas as gerações e todos os nichos - todo mundo gostaria de ter mais atenção, mais concentração e mais serendipidade na vida. O que varia muito é como isso acontece. Quais rituais alguém pode incorporar ao seu dia a dia? Qual a periodicidade ideal desses encontros? Qual a atmosfera perfeita para proporcionar aquilo que alguém mais precisa? Assim como fazem com o seu conteúdo, seja lifestyle, seja desenvolvimento profissional, a curadoria e capacidade de simplificar informações dos creators tem muito valor aqui. O que nos traz ao próximo ponto. 3 - O tal do repertório, que nunca se falou tanto em construir, mas que não está nos mesmos vídeos ou carrosseis virais que todo mundo está compartilhando. Repertório é o que se traduz em uma perspectiva única que só aquela pessoa consegue trazer, com base em tudo que ela carrega consigo. Textos, imagens, experiências, tudo aquilo que você já viu e vivenciou, o lugar da onde você vem, os lugares por onde já passou, as boas conversas, os livros fáceis ou difíceis, os hábitos diários e ambientes que frequenta… Tudo isso forma o seu repertório. Que pode ser composto, sim, pelo que passa pelo feed e vai morar na sua pasta de “salvos” ou no mosaico mental de referências que você acessa a cada job. Mas um ponto de vista realmente original não vem de consumir mais do mesmo, ou apenas o que é filtrado por algoritmos. Vem de uma vida interessante o suficiente para influenciar tudo que você faz. Uma vida que acontece através de telas, mas principalmente fora delas. Naqueles ambientes em que conseguimos estar presentes com todo o nosso corpo (não apenas os nossos dedos em contato com uma tela fria). Naqueles momentos em que uma informação é registrada não porque é vista, mas porque é vivida, com todas as nuances do ambiente, das pessoas que estão ali e de como ela é apresentada. No conhecimento que alguém realmente tem para passar - sem ferramentas que escrevem roteiros, sem a chance de regravar até ficar bom o suficiente. Nas trocas que a gente não consegue pensar antes de digitar ou gravar duas ou três vezes antes de enviar. Depois de anos cronicamente online, é por essas e outras que o conteúdo, a influência e as comunidades têm buscado o offline. _ Quando “comunidade” era a grande tendência nos relatórios, a gente se tornava uma. Quando carrosséis anunciavam o retorno das revistas impressas, a nossa já estava na gráfica. Quando certos produtos físicos estavam virando colecionáveis, o nosso boné esgotou em 24 horas. Agora, chegou a vez da gente olhar para o offline - como movimento de mercado e necessidade humana - do único jeito que a gente sabe fazer: ✨ na prática ✨ Topam ser uma comunidade presencial também? :) Nosso encontro está marcado no dia 27 de outubro, terça-feira, na Avenida Paulista. Com direito a revista impressa e convidados mais que especiais. As vagas são limitadas, e o cupom NEWSLETTER dá 15% de desconto para as dez primeiras pessoas vindas aqui da news: vem para o Bits Ao Vivo para inspirar ✨ A marca americana Altra Running anunciou o seu Altra Legacy Team - a equipe de corrida mais velha do mundo. Juntos, eles têm 321 anos de idade. E querem provar que o objetivo não é correr mais rápido. E sim, seguir correndo. O vídeo do making of da campanha é sensacional. para fazer parte da conversa 💬 O resultado do primeiro turno das eleições foi um grande chá revelação de que vivemos em bolhas. Imprevisível pelas pesquisas, ele demonstrou o retorno do fenômeno “22 confirma”, que elegeu candidatos de postura e currículo extremamente questionáveis sob o guarda-chuva do bolsonarismo. Para refletir sobre o voto que ainda temos a dar neste segundo turno: Quem ocupa as cadeiras do Legislativo em 2027 , uma análise em gráficos Bolsonarismo ou anti-petismo? , um episódio do podcast Café da Manhã A Guerra à Santa , mini-documentário sobre a história (e politização) de Nossa Senhora Aparecida _ “ Cutewashing ”. A Meta e a OpenAI lançaram agentes de IA com nomes e identidades visuais muito fofas. Isso é um estudo de caso de branding, de como a forma com que uma tecnologia é apresentada faz toda diferença em como ela será adotada pelas pessoas. Voltaremos no assunto em breve, mas para quem quiser abrir algumas abas desde já: Por que as big tech querem que agentes de IA sejam os novos labubu Empresas de tecnologia lançam mascotes fofos para aliviar a ansiedade com a IA para continuar a conversa nas redes sociais e convidar mais gente para cá, compartilhe usando o botão abaixo ou marcando a @bitstobrands Share para ler com calma 📄 A gente costumava fazer logoff Diretamente do Pinterest, relatório de tendências em beleza e tendências em hobbies Precisamos olhar para o Brasil mesmo quando é difícil “Não acredito em celebrar o país apenas quando o mundo lá fora está falando bem da gente. Acho que nosso compromisso é outro. É estudar o Brasil e tentar compreendê-lo, embora talvez nunca consigamos inteiramente. É um exercício constante”. para mais conteúdo 📚 🖼️ siga a Bits no Instagram [link] 📚 confira uma seleção de livros na nossa biblioteca [link] 🎧 ouça o podcast Tudo que Importa [link] 🤝 anuncie na Bits - peça o nosso mídia kit em contato@bitstobrands.com 📩 assine essa newsletter , caso não tenha recebido por e-mail :) Subscribe now para dar um tchau 👋🏼 Semana passada, em Vitória, um grupo animado de leitoras da Bits pediu uma foto depois de uma palestra. Sorrindo, uma delas se aproximou dizendo “eu sou muito fã, eu acompanho a newsletter desde quando era você que escrevia!!!”. Eu imagino que essa impressão vem do fato de que a Bits agora tem um time, e tem muito mais projetos e canais do que quando eu comecei uma newsletter nas madrugadas CLT. Mas esse espaço bem aqui, na sua caixa de entrada, onde tudo começou, é pra onde eu faço questão de voltar. Pessoalmente, sem assistente de IA, digitando cada palavra. É tão escrita por mim no alto das suas 307 edições, que a sua frequência está tão maluca quanto a rotina de idas e vindas pelo aeoporto de Congonhas. Mas eu sempre volto. Nem que seja com uma leitura para o fim de semana :) E, claro, um convite mais que especial! - Bia

title: The two forces that help build opportunity
description: Hey pals, I hope all is good in your world. Today we are going to dive a little deeper into two very important elements that build recognisable reputations and brands… and why I built the Opportunity Design Course + Course Club (Early Bird enrollment closes this Sunday!). The two elements? Perception & Evidence. Firstly I want to explain what these two things are individually. Evidence: This is what you’ve actually done. It’s the real, tangible proof of your work. The products you’ve built, the testimonials you’ve earned from your clients, the projects you’ve delivered to your people, the impact you’ve created as a whole. It’s the truth, the receipts, the stuff that stands up in a court of freaking law. Perception: This is what people think you’ve done. It’s how your brand is experienced from the outside. It’s the story that forms in someone’s head long before they ever meet you, talk to you, or work with you. Simply put... Evidence = what is true and provable. Perception = what people believe to be true based on what they can see. The big old problem we all have as creative humans, especially those who have been in the game for a fair chunk of time... it’s impossible for anyone to have access to ALL of your evidence. Most people won’t see the hours you’ve poured in a project, the thinking behind your decisions, or how much bloody effort goes into what you do every damn day. They often just see the end result and that’s where their opinion forms. That’s why perception, in many cases, outweighs evidence... and why perception is super important in brand building. You could be absolutely brilliant at what you do, but if nobody knows it, it doesn’t exist in their world. You might have the work to back it up, but if the way you show up looks sloppy or inconsistent... or you do not show up at all... people will think twice and find another option. That doesn’t mean perception is about pretending or faking it for the internet or your clients in general. It’s about making it easier for people to find the truth, and to do that, you need to give them access to your evidence. Our job as humans who own businesses is to make sure the perception of us from the outside aligns with the truth as closely as possible. Trust doesn’t come from either perception or evidence on its own… it grows when the two work together, and as you can see from the image below, that’s when you become a Power Brand. I personally believe we are all striving to become the “Power Brand” where our perception and evidence are high and in alignment, and the gap between them is very small. This is where true value is created and we become a much safer commercial choice for our clients. Opportunity happens consistently when the truth and perceived reality are best mates, standing together. Here is a little breakdown of each quadrant so you can understand where you might sit. High perception, high evidence: The Power Brand. People notice you and consistently experience the quality behind the perception. Your reputation matches the reality of what you actually deliver, which creates trust, momentum, and long-term opportunity. Every great brand we know masters this balance between perception and evidence. High perception, low evidence: The Hype Brand. You know how to grab attention and create excitement, but the reality underneath hasn’t fully caught up yet. Things can look bigger, stronger, or more established from the outside than they actually are once people get closer. Low perception, high evidence: The Hidden Genius Brand. You’re doing brilliant work, but not enough people currently get the chance to experience it. The skill, care, and trustworthiness are already there… your reputation just hasn’t spread far beyond your existing network yet. (I built Opportunity Design for you my friends) Low perception, low evidence: The Work-in-Progress Brand. You’re still figuring things out, experimenting, learning, and discovering where your strengths actually live. And honestly? That’s completely normal. Every powerful brand, business, and creative human starts as a work in progress. The big takeaway here? Branding isn’t just about reality... it’s also about perceived reality. People can’t choose you based on the evidence they have never seen. They can only choose you based on what they know, and ultimately, believe to be true about you. This is why I am so excited about The Opportunity Design Course + Course Club that starts next week. This is a 6-week programme designed to help you close the gap between what you’re capable of and what other people know you’re capable of, in order to create more extraordinary opportunities. title: #306 | Uma seleção de campanhas
description: nas edições anteriores #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1) #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2) tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 A essa altura você já sabe que a Bits to Brands virou uma revista impressa . Duas, na verdade, considerando que estamos na segunda edição. Já somos praticamente uma banca. O que você talvez não saiba é que este processo criativo começou lá em 2014, quando a gente visualizou uma revista impressa que viria com um boné, feita para ser a companhia ideal para o verão de 2025. (Por isso a garota da capa estava sentada em uma cadeira de praia lendo uma revista, que dentro tinha uma página só de palavras cruzadas e vinha com um cartão postal retratando um dia de praia…) Ou seja: não basta selecionar os artigos, ordenar e diagramar de forma que faça sentido e pensar o projeto gráfico - toda revista precisa ter um tema. _ Na sua segunda edição, em 2026, o escolhido foi Bora de Brasil . Uma das grandes tendências do ano, e um tema de grande interesse por aqui - das pesquisas traduzindo a nossa cultura à possibilidade de contar mais histórias de marcas brasileiras. Imagina não ser brasileiro e não reparar no rodinho de pia? A celebração da brasilidade foi o norte para a capa, o título, as cores, a curadoria de artigos e, claro, para a experiência memorável que a gente quer que a revista seja. Aqui a gente não coloca impresso no mundo para ir parar no fundo da gaveta. Ou é para guardar, ou é para expor, ou é para interagir. Ou quem sabe até todas as anteriores. É por isso que, dessa vez, ela tem uma lombada quadrada (fica melhor na estante) , tem uma página que vira pôster (um lembrete para a sua área de trabalho) e tem um álbum de figurinhas. _ Brasilidade + impresso + offline + Copa do Mundo. A cada quatro anos essas referências se encontram na sensação de completar, uma de cada vez, dezenas de páginas de um álbum. As figurinhas, por sua vez, trazem imagens conhecidas, reconhecidas, algumas até icônicas, que representam o melhor do país naquela modalidade. A nossa modalidade é o marketing. A nossa seleção, portanto, é composta de ações de marcas que destacam o melhor da criatividade brasileira nas últimas décadas. Fiquem agora com a nossa Seleção, na certeza de que ela deixou grandes destaques de fora. Porém com a esperança de que isso gere bons debates e trocas. _ Em 2013, a Kombi contava em primeira pessoa as histórias reais que as pessoas enviaram para celebrar a sua despedida. Em 1998, a Johnson’s Baby reforçava a sua linha de shampoos infantis, e oferecia a trilha sonora para milhões de banhos de bebês dali em diante. Em 2019, o McDonald’s deixava de lado a consistência em nome do seu real significado (e grafia) para o público brasileiro. Em 1997, dois pequenos esquimós transformavam Danoninho em sorvetinho, e a gente ganhava uma frase para repetir por décadas. Em 2025, a Red Bull transformava um edifício icônico de Porto Alegre em rampa para um dos maiores skatistas do Brasil. Em 2011, alguns pôneis cantavam em volta de um carro Nissan , em um dos virais mais marcantes do início das redes sociais. Em 2020, a Netflix esgotava em algumas horas uma edição especial impressa do seu universo de conteúdo. Em 1991, uma série de conteúdos transformava uma marca em adjetivo e fazia muita gente se questionar se qualquer coisa era ou não era “assim uma Brastemp ”... Em 2025, o Canva colocou a Xuxa em um dos seus figurinos icônicos para lançar uma linha de produtos e uma campanha especial “para adultinhos”. _ Além de uma Seleção de Campanhas, a Revista Bits to Brands tem 50 páginas de conteúdo e ilustrações. Ela é a materialização da nossa identidade visual e conteúdo, e também daquilo que a gente acredita: o poder das palavras, a conexão para além das telas e o valor que as coisas ganham quando passam a fazer parte da vida real de alguém. Para viabilizar o seu envio para diferentes cantos do Brasil, estamos fazendo uma tiragem especial em forma de produto social. Você pode garantir a sua pelo valor de R$ 79,90 - e todo o lucro desta ação será destinado a uma ONG de incentivo à leitura no Brasil. Esperamos que seja uma boa leitura, uma ótima surpresa e algo significativo e duradouro como só o impresso é capaz de se tornar. E O Boticário mostrou que uma boa estratégia de comunicação acontece entre o online e o offline, agregando ao entretenimento ao invés de interrompê-lo. Durante a novela Quem Ama Cuida, a marca foi inserida em meio a dois personagens que representam o seu principal atributo: intensidade. Na cena, amostras do novo hidratante são usadas e mencionadas de forma sutil. Só no break comercial que a mensagem se completa: dobro de ameixa, dobro de amostras nas lojas. title: #303 | Marcas multiespécie
description: nas edições anteriores #301 | O legado da Copa do Mundo 2026 #302 | Os oráculos da timeline tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 Segundo o estudo Tendências Brasil 2026, de Globo Gente: Pela primeira vez, casais com filhos são menos da metade das famílias do país; Lares unipessoais, casais com pets e uniões homoafetivas cresceram vertiginosamente; O número de pessoas que moram sozinhas triplicou de 2000 para 2022. _ É neste contexto que os animais de estimação têm ganhado status (e padrão de vida) de filhos em muitas casas brasileiras. Plano de saúde, guarda-roupas para todas as estações do ano, festas de aniversário, creches e escolas, entretenimento… Em uma economia que que movimenta um estimado de R$ 77 bilhões por ano. Quando novas configurações de família são cada vez mais “multiespécie”, esses códigos passam a fazer parte da comunicação de todo tipo de categoria. Todo mundo percebeu que falar com “pais de pet” é estratégico na busca pela atenção, cada vez mais escassa, e da conexão emocional, cada vez mais dispersa. O fator “fofo” é capaz de reter as pessoas por mais tempo, enquanto gera uma reação imediata - curtir, comentar, compartilhar e, claro, comprar. Segundo dados da Buzzmonitor, o aumento no engajamento com publicações que contém pets é de 16%. É por essas e outras que temos visto pets em todos os lugares. De montadoras de carro a fast-food (sim). Sendo público-alvo de novos produtos, influenciadores das suas causas ou apenas “bichinhos propaganda”. O movimento que impulsionou o crescimento de diversas empresas do segmento pet, agora atinge todas as que sabem aproveitá-lo. Marcas que estão se tornando multiespécie. _ O Grupo Boticário levou a sua experiência em perfumaria e desenvolvimento de produtos para uma marca dedicada a deixar a rotina com cães e gatos mais cheirosa. A Stanley lançou o Pet Bowl, feito do mesmo material dos seus produtos que retém temperaturas, para manter a água dos bichinhos gelada e evitar o uso de plástico no seu dia a dia. A Rimowa agora também tem a Pet Carrier Bag, uma bolsa para transporte de animais até 8kg que, além do cuidado no conforto e design, é feita para se acoplar às malas da marca. Até o McDonald’s está pensando no bem-estar desses membros da família. Não lanches especiais (ainda), mas com uma embalagem lançada em Singapura - a Happy Meow Bag é um brinquedo para gatos inspirado nos pacotes do restaurante. _ E talvez o maior sinal das mudanças em como representamos “família” e a inclusão dos pets na estratégia das mais diversas marcas, esteja no segmento de carros. Houve um tempo em que falar de SUVs era sinônimo de imagens de carros grandes com crianças no banco de trás e muitas malas indo pegar a estrada. Hoje, quem está sendo transportado é o cachorro. Ano passado, para lançar o novo modelo da Tracker, a Chevrolet trouxe o vira-lata caramelo como protagonista da sua campanha. Além do filme publicitário, aproveitou o hype do filme Caramelo, na Netflix, para ações em redes sociais. E essa semana mesmo, a Peugeot lançou o E-5008 Dog Edition, com funcionalidades e acessórios focados no conforto dos pets. _ Basicamente, depois de criar uma indústria inteira em torno de si, os animais de estimação agora estão conquistando espaço em marcas de todos os segmentos. Pets atraem o olhar, inspiram emoção e tornam qualquer comunicação mais memorável. Mas a sua presença é mais do que um atalho no jogo da atenção. Ela é reflexo de um novo contexto social e uma nova ideia de família. Num presente que deixa isso cada vez mais evidente, e um futuro que não mostra qualquer sinal de que isso mude. title: #302 | Os oráculos da timeline
description: nas edições anteriores #300 | A vida das coisas #301 | O legado da Copa do Mundo 2026 tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 do dicionário: oráculo, substantivo masculino Num lugar sagrado, resposta a uma pergunta feita a uma divindade cujo teor era entendido como profético, sendo de difícil compreensão, obscuro. Resposta dada por uma divindade, quando alguém a consultava. Pessoa que, supostamente, prevê o futuro ou a previsão feita por essa pessoa. _ Nada contra carrosseis de Instagram. Inclusive, fazemos vários. O formato inicialmente permitia compartilhar dez imagens em um único post, e depois foi expandido para vinte. Primeiro, foi utilizado pelos millennials como álbum do Orkut - registros agrupados de um mesmo evento. Depois a gen Z, querendo performar menos, intercalou fotos posadas com fotos aleatórias e chamou de dump . Enquanto isso, a bolha criadora de conteúdo tratava as telas como slides e elaborava apresentações sobre todo tipo de assunto - com call to action no final, claro. Salve, compartilhe, assine, contrate, inscreva-se. O carrossel é um dos formatos preferidos de quem busca engajamento. Basta um questionamento bem amplo e chamativo na capa, seguido por uma série de telas que ora explicam, ora confundem. O resultado é a banalização de questões extremamente profundas - como se a resposta coubesse em um carrossel de Instagram. Ou como se eles fossem de fato lidos com a devida atenção, ou escritos com a pretensão de elaborar uma pauta para além do rage bait da capa. Como se eles fossem sequer escritos por uma outra pessoa. _ Nada contra carrosseis de Instagram. Inclusive, fazemos vários. É muito útil poder intercalar explicações com imagens, organizar textos de forma compartilhável, ampliar discussões e aumentar a audiência sem depender de vídeos curtos. A inteligência artificial é uma grande aliada nesta organização de informações e layout para expressar ideias. Agora, a disseminação dos carrosseis feitos por inteligência artificial, posicionando suas fontes como oráculos contemporâneos das gerações, do brasileiro ou de qualquer tipo de comportamento tem servido mais para vender, do que para informar. No grande mercado que virou a timeline, a atual recomendação é juntar o questionamento profundo com a elaboração rasa e o call to action certo no final. Assim, vamos arrastando para cima de uma pergunta para outra e delegando a nossa capacidade de reflexão ao marketing digital. De repente, parece que questões complexas cabem nesse tipo de generalização, que gerações inteiras podem ser reduzidas a frases de efeito, ou que estratégias elaboradas podem ser decifradas em algumas telas. _ Perguntas são feitas desde que o mundo é mundo. A busca por respostas, inclusive, talvez seja mais importante na nossa evolução do que o momento em que elas são encontradas. Seguir sem respostas talvez seja uma das coisas mais inspiradoras que existem. O que muda é o contexto em que perguntas surgem e respostas são elaboradas. title: Join My Free Mentorship Program
description: My friends, Over 20+ years in the creative industry, I’ve seen (and weathered) a lot of its ups and downs… new tech, social media, changing economies… These days, the creative industry is shifting big again, and the people feeling it most are the ones just starting out. Which, let’s be honest, is pretty shit. Students, juniors, early-stage creatives… you’re not just being squeezed financially, you’re carrying the mental side of it too. You’re constantly being told you’re replaceable. That AI is coming for your job. That the thing you’ve spent years learning might not matter anymore. And after a while, that kind of noise starts to play gams with the old brain. But, a lot of this noise is lazy thinking at best, because there is no future creative industry without creative people. title: The Industry Swap Experiment
description: An amazingly random thing happened this last week. I found myself in Moab, Utah, with around 70 total strangers who now feel like my best friends. I was invited by my buddy Jason to speak at the first-ever Summer Camp hosted by his company, Rupt, for the promotional products industry. There were team colours, a healthy dose of friendly competition, prizes, adventures and learning sessions, all set against the incredible backdrop of the Colorado River and the red rock desert. It was fucking Magical. As a brand guy I often find myself around brand people whether thats agency owners, designers or people building things in the creative space but I have always loved to pop myself in the deep water of the unknowing. I know very little about this world. Like most people, I’ve interacted with the industry countless times as an end user. Whether that’s branded merch, company swag, event giveaways or promotional products arriving in the post… but I’ve never actually spent too much time inside the industry itself or with the people who make it all happen… so on paper, I had absolutely no business being there. But that’s exactly why I jumped at the chance to speak at this event. I love learning new things, and this room was packed with some of the biggest hitters in the game. People who have spent years building businesses and solving problems in a world I know jack shit about. It would have been easy to say no. The travel was long, the industry was unfamiliar but saying no to this opportunity was never really on the cards for me. I am getting older, and as that happens, the more I think one of the biggest mistakes we make is only learning from people who do the same thing as us. We all read the same design books, follow pretty much the same people, attend the same conferences and end up having the same conversations over and over again. This felt like the exact opposite of that… I’m gonna call it the ‘anti-echo chamber’ move. An opportunity to step outside my own little corner of the world and spend time with people who think differently and see things through a completely different lens. I had a feeling it would open my brain up in ways it hadn’t been before, and it absolutely did. Now, even though this space doesn’t live and breathe design in the same way mine does, it still lives in the world of branding. Most brand people spend their time on the fun stuff like the thinking, story, and execution side of design. We help make strategic decisions, build the identity, and create the funky punky assets. Then, more often than not, we release the work into the wild and hope it finds its way. What really hit home for me whilst spending time with this incredible group of humans is that this industry is actually much closer to mine than I first realised. They’re positioned at an incredibly important point in the journey… where the identity of a company meets real humans in the real world. They are a key part of what we do because they help bring businesses to life through experiences. And ultimately, that’s where ‘brand status’ is earned. As brand people, we’re in the game of pattern building and memory. We help businesses become recognisable. The promotional products industry helps those companies show up in the real world, creating physical touch-points and experiences that reinforce everything the business is trying to stand for. The biggest takeaway for me this week, apart from the fact that Moab might be one of the coolest places on the planet, is that every industry has its own wisdom. Every industry has people solving interesting problems and has a lot of knowledge to offer the general outsider who is keen to learn a new perspective. It’s easy to convince ourselves that all the answers live inside our own little bubble, but I’ve found over the years that many of the best ideas and implementations in my own business have come from looking outside of design. Whether that’s borrowing hospitality thinking and applying it to my design process, or building an identity of my own that fuses tattoo culture with skate-shop vibes, the things that have helped me stand out have not come from simply doing what everyone else was doing. One of the ideas I shared during my talk was Hotelling’s Law … the observation that competitors naturally drift towards sameness because it feels safer. Over time, everyone starts looking similar, sounding similar and offering similar things because nobody wants to stray too far from what appears to be working for others. The irony though is that the safest thing to do often becomes the riskiest thing to do. If everybody moves towards the middle, the middle becomes really freaking crowded. Which is why I’ve always been more interested in pushing at the edges… That’s where the interesting opportunities live. That’s why I think we should all spend a little more time making anti-echo chamber moves. Here are some ways you can do that: 1. Go to the event that isn’t built for you. 2. Read the book that nobody in your industry is talking about. 3. Spend time with people who challenge your assumptions. 4. Put yourself in rooms where you’re not the expert. Remember, my friends… curiosity is often where the magic lives. And if my week in the Utah desert taught me anything, it’s that sometimes the most valuable thing you can do isn’t go deeper into your own world… It’s to spend some time exploring somebody else’s. Big love and respect. James - The People’s Branding Mentor

title: Tiny moments that become a real brand.
description: Before we jump into this week’s article, reminder that my new book No Bullsh*t Branding is available for pre-order… and if you pre-order by the end of today (Sunday 31st May) you get a bonus freebie bundle, including the Book Club, the new MVB Course, limited edition MBJ merch, and digital downloads. Check it out here ! Thank you all so much for your support. Last weekend the weather was delicious. So delicious that myself, Kate and Rocco went to the beach for the day to hang with our friends (Jamie & Mel) and their little kiddos… it was one of those beautiful little days that will live long in the memory bank. We were down at West Wittering beach near Chichester. It’s this big, magical stretch of sand where, when the tide goes out, the beach becomes absolutely colossal. Perfect for kids because there’s endless space to run around and play… it becomes the worlds largest, sandy adventure space. Scattered across the beach are these little pools of warm water left behind by the retreating tide… tiny, stinky lakes full of seaweed, shells, wet sand and mess. Basically heaven for a little dude like Rocco. And he was more than happy exploring them completely alone while the rest of his friends sat further up the beach eating lunch and digging holes. He was so happy, so I wanted him to just ‘be’… so I stayed and watched. After maybe an hour of watching him play in the same giant puddle, I eventually wandered up to him and asked him to come back to “base camp” so we could put more suncream on, tag mummy back in and potentially allow me to eat some lunch. But he was having absolutely none of it. Everything I offered was ignored. Every negotiation tactic I’d learned in business was useless, and every attempt to reason with him about how the sun was really hot and he needed protecting from it was completely pointless. Eventually Kate, my wonderful wife, spotted my slow descent into parental defeat from afar and wandered over with all the supplies we needed. And at that point, I just accepted reality and decided to play the waiting game until he was ready to move on himself… I mean, the sun would go down eventually, I was sure of that, and I also now had a sandwich. But there was a lesson hiding inside all of this. When you have very little to negotiate with, the situation you are in becomes incredibly difficult to win… and this got me thinking about the very beginning of my own business journey. It was so difficult to find any money-making opportunities when I started because I had so little to negotiate with. No Leverage. I had no real portfolio, no website, no testimonials and, in absolute honesty… very little knowledge. I wouldn’t have hired me. As you know, for me, a brand is a recognisable reputation, and at that point I was neither recognised nor did I really have a reputation worth knowing… unless it was “having a good time down the pub” - I was real good at that. And this got me thinking about all the newbies entering the world right now. All the junior creatives trying to find work and carve out a place for themselves while also navigating challenges I never had to deal with. Things like social media pressure, constant comparison, AI, tech and the heavy, heavy, heavy psychological weight of feeling like you need to live your life so publicly online. Now, I’m not saying my era had it easy at all… every generation has its own struggles. But I do think it’s harder now than it was 20 years ago, mainly for the reasons I mentioned above. So I want to try an answer this question today. How do we build a business when, right at the beginning, we have nothing to be recognised for and no reputation backing us up? So… lets chat. Yes, you might not have the clients yet. You might not have the case studies, the swanky portfolio, the testimonials or the years of industry proof backing up your ambition. But what you do have is YOU. That matters far more than many people think. Because there are already so many things you are recognised for outside of your “business circles”. Your attitude, your energy, your humour, your kindness, your curiosity, your willingness to help, your ability to make people feel good around you, your ability to stay optimistic when everything feels difficult or half empty. What I’m trying to suggest here is that even if you do not yet have a recognisable reputation around your work, you already have years and years of building a recognisable reputation around your humanness and character, and that is a beautifully fun place to start… that becomes your negotiating power. One of the huge advantages early stage creatives have is that they are not yet boxed in by the “rules” of the industry. They are not trapped by client expectations or weighed down by years of process refinement and predictability. They still have “all the raws”… raw energy, raw enthusiasm and raw creativity to boot. In the beginning, it’s often your willingness to care about others and build relationships that sparks the most opportunity. Helping a mate out for freebies, offering your services to friends of friends in exchange for tickets to their latest gig… that scrappy little world of free crafty goodness is where most of us cut our teeth in the industry. When I was starting out, I bartered constantly. I used my skills to build experience, and the more experience I gained, the more confidence I built. In return, I’d get free coffee, free jewellery, free food, whilst also building relationships with local humans… whatever people could offer at the time instead of money, I said yes to. Looking back, I actually think there’s something incredibly beautiful about that stage of the journey. I mean, bartering is how worlds were built. When you’re starting out, you still have permission to try almost anything you can to keep the lights on and keep the dream alive. You can knock on doors, start conversations, help people, make things, experiment, build fabulous little ditties and push your creativity out into the world. And over time, people begin recognising you for those behaviours. For your energy, your effort, your generosity, your consistency and the way you make people feel. Almost without noticing it, those tiny moments become the foundations of a recognisable reputation. A real brand. So if you are at the beginning, listening to a noisy world telling you that “designers are fucked” or “the creative industry is doomed,” remember that most of it is just distraction… like a lot of news on the inter webs. Don’t fall into the trap of blindly listening to these people. Many of them have their own agenda too… which is often making sure they stay relevant and irreplaceable in a changing world. Instead, use your creativity and your energy to build relationships. Make cool stuff and send it to people. Write a little hand-drawn note thanking somebody for inspiring you. Instead of sending the same PDF portfolio to 400 people like everybody else is doing, start more real, human conversations. Barter your services. Collaborate with people. Send a hand written letter. Deliver someone a little product with your work on it. Go above and beyond simply because you care enough to do so. Become recognised for how much effort you are putting in… that is a reputation that opportunities will eventually flow towards. Stay Focused, Stay Crafty… Your creativity is your super duper power. James - The Peoples Branding Mentor

title: The Unscriptable Moments That Build Reputation
description: Hello my champions of creative goodness. How are ya? Today I want to dive into a little topic that I am super passionate about, and that is the human goodness we can do to elevate the experience for the people we work with. Everyone reading this is a craft-based, creativity-infused builder of things. You might own a business, work with brands, or create cool visuals for people who love looking at cool visuals. I don’t think creative people like that need motivation to continue doing the things they already do so well, but I do think there is another layer we often forget to think about… the human layer. The stuff on top of the craft. That is where some new magic can be found. It looks like over the coming years a lot of businesses and brands will automate huge parts of their customer journey, which is logical, so the question for me becomes… Where does the human come in and make a decision that was not obvious? I am all for becoming more efficient and dialling in a good process, as many of you will know, but it’s often the stupid-on-paper, “not good for business” decisions that build a reputation worth talking about. One of my favourite examples of human creativity elevating a brand’s reputation is the story of Joshie the Giraffe. A family went on holiday to California and accidentally left their son’s stuffed giraffe at a Ritz-Carlton hotel where they were staying. To put the little boy at ease, his dad told a little white lie and said Joshie had decided to stay behind for an extra holiday. The dad had phoned the hotel and asked if they could find it, send it back, and hopefully reunite the little guy with his giraffe. The hotel staff found Joshie amongst the laundry and could have simply posted the toy back. But instead, they created an entire photo album showing Joshie relaxing by the pool, driving golf carts, getting spa treatments with cucumbers over his eyes, and “enjoying his extended vacation” before finally sending him home, all to back up his dad’s story. That tiny, unscriptable moment of human creativity transformed a forgotten toy into a story that millions of people still talk about today… just like I am right now. And I think that’s freaking fascinating. Because I doubt that family remembers much about the facilities at the Ritz-Carlton, the weather, or even how good the food was… but they will absolutely remember Joshie’s holiday forever. This got the old curiosity up… Why do moments like this stick with us so deeply while so many other experiences disappear from memory almost immediately? Why do we instantly want to tell our mates about them, repost them online and emotionally connect with complete strangers because of them? For that we probably need to get a little ‘sciencey’. Now remember, I’m not a scientist. I’m just an inquisitive bloke with a scraggly beard who spends far too much time researching human behaviour, but here’s what I found out… Your brain is basically a very clever prediction machine. Most of the time, your brain is trying to conserve energy by guessing what is about to happen next based on previous experiences and familiar patterns. If things go exactly as expected, the brain doesn’t need to pay much attention because nothing new or important is happening. Win for brain power. This is why most of our routine experiences disappear from memory almost immediately. If you are anything like me, you get in the car, drive somewhere you’ve been a thousand times before, pull up, get out, and suddenly realise you barely even remember the journey itself. You obviously drove, stopped at traffic lights and avoided crashing into things, but because your brain already knew the pattern, most of the drive happened on complete autopilot… and it’s even easier now I don’t have to change gears anymore. Thank fook for the automatic. Humans do this constantly. We predict things, filter things and automate familiar experiences because if we had to consciously process every tiny detail of every moment of every day we would mentally collapse before our cheeky 11am coffee break. That’s why so many experiences we go through every single day become, well… forgettable. You expect the hotel room to be ready when you arrive. You expect somebody at reception to hand you a key, point you towards the lift or stairs and solve any mini problems in the quickest and most logical way possible, so when all of those things happen exactly as predicted, your brain simply processes the experience efficiently and moves on because nothing emotionally interesting actually happened. But when something interrupts that predictable pattern in a creative, emotional or unexpected way, your brain suddenly pays far more attention because it wasn’t expecting it. That’s why the Joshie story mattered so freaking much. The family expected the hotel to find the giraffe and simply post it back. Problem solved. No dramas here people. Everybody moves on with their lives. But instead, the hotel staff created this ridiculously brilliant, fake holiday for the giraffe that made it feel like Joshie was genuinely out there living his best life in the California sun and making mates along the way. They went to completely unreasonable measures just to bring a little bit of joy to a child and back up his dad’s white lie, and that exact unpredictability is what made the whole thing unforgettable. Humans remember meaningful and surprising moments far more than they remember predictable and functional ones. The hotel didn’t just solve the problem. They transformed a completely ordinary customer service interaction into a story that people are still retelling years later… and I think that’s the bit most of us miss as business owners. People rarely remember what was efficient, but they almost always remember how something made them feel. I mean, I almost bloody cried the first time I read the Joshie story because I instantly thought about how my own son would feel seeing his favourite toy off living its best life and making mates on holiday. I take Lightning McQueen with me on work trips because I miss my son Rocco, and I take silly little photos of him at random places because I know my son lights up when he sees them. He genuinely thinks daddy and Lightning are away together having a good time, so this little giraffe story hit a proper emotional note for me. The Joshie story stopped being “good customer service” and instantly became something far more human because you could feel the love, effort and humanity inside the decision those hotel staff made… and that kind of creativity can never be automated. Nor bloody should it. I hope this story sparks the creativity inside you to go against the grain when you can. To be unpredictable with your kindness and to find ways to connect with others that might be out of the ordinary. People remember people who thought about them in different and unique ways. I think, over the coming years, businesses and brands will increasingly be judged on what they choose to keep human. Automate the predictable. Humanise the meaningful. Love ya. James - The People’s Branding Mentor

title: #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2)
description: nas edições anteriores #303 | Marcas multiespécie #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1) tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 Passamos os últimos dois anos falando, desejando, criando, repetindo o termo “offline” nos nossos planos de mídia e carrosseis de Instagram, a ponto dele ter se tornado também um grande hype . Por um lado, pessoas performando atividades online apenas para postar. Por outro, marcas usando esse movimento como desculpa pra poluir visualmente o mundo real ou encher as nossas casas de objetos desnecessários. (Nem tudo deveria ter um anúncio. O mundo não precisa de mais um brinde com o seu logo sem intenção nenhuma). E agora? _ Este não é um manifesto anti-offline. De maneira alguma. A gente não deve desistir de materializar as nossas marcas ou criar experiências no mundo real (não vamos desistir) . Mas neste processo, é importante entender duas coisas: 1. “Offline é o novo luxo” é uma maneira muito simplista de olhar para essa tendência. Ela é indiscutivelmente atrativa para as marcas de luxo, que sempre pautaram a sua comunicação na estética e estilos de vida capazes de diferenciar as pessoas. Quando a estética “comum” é cronicamente online, feita por IA e vidrada em uma tela, o luxo busca ilustrações feitas à mão e experiências sensoriais. Mas a necessidade de desconectar vai além da performance e da distinção social. O que torna o “offline” um movimento muito maior que qualquer trend é justamente a sua capacidade de resgatar uma série de aspectos que têm se perdido na vida moderna. A presença, a atenção, o processo, o aprendizado, a conexão com outras pessoas, a dificuldade (e, consequentemente, a resiliência)… E as tantas sensações, rituais e habilidades que só o mundo real proporciona. Objetos físicos, eventos e atividades manuais devem seguir parte da estratégia das marcas. Não para gerar percepção de luxo ou para fazer igual a uma ou outra. Muito menos para criar novos espaços de mídia que “chamam mais atenção”. E sim pela sua capacidade de interromper o scroll infinito, de ser um lembrete da vida que acontece fora das telas, de gerar valor e, quem sabe, até transformação real nas pessoas. O que nos leva ao segundo ponto. _ 2. Quando o offline se torna hype, é preciso fugir do lugar comum Em 2025, fizemos a primeira edição de uma revista impressa. Ela foi a realização de um sonho antigo, e a materialização da Bits to Brands em cores, ilustrações e páginas enviadas para todo o Brasil. Seu projeto editorial foi feito em outubro de 2024, e a sua impressão em dezembro. Na época, as revistas já começavam a despontar como símbolo de nostalgia - mas não dava para imaginar que seria um movimento tão intenso. Desde então, diversas marcas imprimiram revistas - e serviram café, receberam clubes do livro, ofereceram corridas de rua, distribuíram bonés bordados, estamparam câmeras analógicas… Assim, apenas na sua segunda edição, uma revista não é mais surpreendente ou inovadora. Do mesmo jeito que, em 2026, um boné também não é. (Aliás, um boné vira parte de uma coleção que está chegando a 20 unidades por aqui) O valor do offline não vai a lugar nenhum, mas fazer o básico não é mais o suficiente. title: #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1)
description: nas edições anteriores #302 | Os oráculos da timeline #303 | Marcas multiespécie tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 Já vai fazer dois anos que a expressão “o offline é o novo luxo” se disseminou pela internet. Ora como análise de tendência, ora como sinalização de virtude. Nós também somos um pouco culpados disso: Em janeiro de 2025, prestes a lançar a primeira edição da nossa revista impressa, estávamos mergulhados no “offline”. E não só a gente. Foi um verão em que muita gente procurou desconectar, e assim seguiu pelas estações. De câmeras analógicas a aulas de cerâmica, palavras cruzadas, telefones fixos… Todo tipo de estratégia (e produto) foi surgindo para ajudar. Começando, inclusive, pelas marcas de luxo. Porque não é uma coincidência que este seja o adjetivo mais utilizado ao lado da palavra “offline”. Tanto porque o “luxo” é mais valioso e raro, quanto porque ele é aquilo que foge do comum. Quando uma estética ou comportamento se torna o básico, aquilo que todo mundo tem, beirando até o “brega” - performar superioridade intelectual e social é se afastar dela. (A relação entre consumo e performance social está super bem explicada em Coisa de Rico , de Michel Alcoforado). Se nos últimos anos o comum é ser hiperconectado, cronicamente online e passar incontáveis horas arrastando para cima imóvel, o que passa a comunicar luxo e status é desconectar. Ler livros de verdade, fazer atividade física ao ar livre, acessórios tecnológicos mais vintage, encontros para discutir temas específicos, o resgate dos hábitos e atividades sociais das avós (do tricô ao nonna-maxxing )… É por essas e outras que a Miu Miu tem um clube do livro, a Bottega Veneta lançou um jogo de Jenga, a Prada fez uma floricultura e as marcas de luxo têm disputado espaço para fazer ativações nos grandes torneios de tênis pelo mundo. O offline se tornou, sim, sinônimo de luxo. Mas não pára por aí. _ O offline se tornou território de desejo das marcas por motivos certos e errados, racionais e abstratos, mas muitos deles ancorados em comportamentos e demandas bem reais. Um deles é a distinção social. Mas ativações no mundo real, eventos, experiências e objetos físicos despertam interesse também porque são comunitários, sensoriais, duráveis, memoráveis e humanos. Cada um desses aspectos parte de demandas da vida contemporânea que começam no excesso de telas, mas se estendem para a ausência de interações sociais, a substituição do corpo físico pela imagem editada de alguém e até o tal “AI Slop”. Num parque a gente não precisa ficar se perguntando se algo é IA ou não a cada dois minutos (ainda). Porque o offline é comunidade , ele nos permite lembrar que não estamos sozinhos nos nossos gostos e hobbies - seja correr uma meia maratona, seja ter sido fã da Xuxa na infância. Porque o offline é sensorial , ele nos lembra que cada um é um corpo, e não apenas um cérebro e as pontas dos dedos. E que um corpo é capaz de sentir gostos, cheiros, toques, de dançar, cantar, esbarrar, ver e ser visto e se relacionar - de verdade. Porque o offline é durável , ele se torna representação no mundo real de quem a gente é. Aquilo que decora os nossos ambientes, que compõe as nossas coleções , que está pendurado nas nossas bolsas e mochilas ou até geladeiras - ajuda a contar a nossa história. Diga-me o que colecionas e te direi quem és. Porque o offline é memorável, ele é uma grande oportunidade para as marcas investirem seus orçamentos de comunicação de forma mais assertiva. Estamos descobrindo que reunir um grupo de pessoas verdadeiramente atentas e interessadas tem mais valor do que atingir milhões de views sabe-se lá de quem. E porque o offline é humano, ele é o único ambiente onde a gente vivencia o tempo de forma linear, a arte de forma artesanal e o mundo conforme a nossa própria curadoria de experiências - e não a de um algortimo. Não é à toa que todo mundo quer mais disso. _ Passamos os últimos dois anos falando, desejando, criando, repetindo o termo “offline” nos nossos planos de mídia e carrosseis de Instagram, a ponto dele ter se tornado também um grande hype . Por um lado, pessoas performando atividades online apenas para postar. Por outro, marcas usando esse movimento como desculpa pra poluir visualmente o mundo real ou encher as nossas casas de objetos desnecessários. (Nem tudo deveria ter um anúncio. O mundo não precisa de mais um brinde com o seu logo sem intenção nenhuma). E agora? _ continua na próxima edição. para continuar a conversa nas redes sociais e convidar mais gente para cá, compartilhe usando o botão abaixo ou marcando a @bitstobrands Share para inspirar ✨ Ao invés de só um case, vocês aceitam três? :) Como parte da nossa estratégia de ser verdadeiramente multicanal (com conteúdo feito para cada plataforma) e inspirar as pessoas por trás das marcas brasileiras e no Brasil, surgiu a #BrasilnaBits. Uma editoria no Instagram para explorar marcas brasileiras de diferentes regiões e segmentos, e tudo que elas têm a nos ensinar. Já passamos por Tramontina , Xeque Mate e Turma da Mônica . E se você tiver sugestões, pode deixar aqui nos comentários. para fazer parte da conversa 💬 O Instagram atualizou a sua tipografia e todo o seu universo visual . E é claro que todo mundo queria ter uma opinião. title: The Personal Brand Trap: Why Humans Shouldn’t Think of Themselves as Brands
description: When I was a wee little boy growing up, I wanted to be a fireman. It seemed considerably more achievable than becoming a ThunderCat or Batman, which were my other career choices when I was eight. At school I had absolutely no clue what I wanted to do as a career. Potentially something arty or sporty, but back in the 90s I was told neither of those were money-makers, so I had to think about getting a proper job. Today, I would classify myself as a designer and educator helping the next generation of creatives build more opportunity for themselves. That feels very aligned with who I am today. But I have also been a barman, factory worker, waiter, tattoo apprentice, window cleaner, failed businessman, unemployable bum, and many other things on the journey to finding this particular version of me. And that is one of the wonderful things about being a human… nobody really freaking knows who they’re going to become. The person you are today is probably very different from the person you were five years ago, and if you’re doing this thing called life properly, there’s a good chance the person you’ll become five years from now will look different again. And, from what my mum tells me… that’s completely normal. Most of us are making it up as we go, collecting experiences and continuously falling forward into newer versions of ourselves… we’re supposed to evolve. So in this little article I want to share my perspective on a topic that I think deserves a little more questioning: personal branding. More specifically, I want to explore why I don’t think humans should think of themselves as brands, and why applying brand logic to a human being can potentially do more harm than good. Thanks for reading The Real Brand Life! Subscribe for free to receive new posts. Now, I’m not here to suggest that personal branding doesn’t exist. That would cause a riot. Instead, I’d like to challenge some of the advice being peddled around willy-nilly on the dopamine drug train that is social media. To do that, I think we first need to agree on the difference between brand logic and human logic. A brand’s job is to reduce complexity. Brands are trying to be recognised at scale and for that to happen, they need to simplify things. They need to make themselves easier to understand, remember and choose. They do that better when they are associated with a couple of very clear ideas. Humans, on the other hand, operate very differently my friends. We change our minds all the freaking time. We become interested in new things. We learn stuff, we grow our minds and then we see the world differently because of it. And an important thing to add is that humans don’t naturally operate at scale. We evolved in small communities and tribes, not in front of thousands of random people online. So if brands become stronger through consistency and humans become stronger through change, are we really sure those two things belong together? That’s why I find phrases like “you are your brand” and “everyone has a personal brand” a little, well… problematic. Being known for something and being a brand are not the same thing. I understand that these phrases are often being used as shortcuts, but even when I account for that nuance, I still think they fundamentally misunderstand what a brand is… and what a human needs. Now, I don’t want this to come across as a rant or a black-and-white argument, as some of the advice coming out of the personal brand camp is incredibly useful. Visibility matters for sure because if nobody knows what the heck you do, how on earth are they supposed to hire you? Other people need to know you exist people. I absolutely believe humans should become known. Known for doing good work, having interesting ideas, standing for something and making a positive impact on the people around them. But becoming known and becoming a product are not the same thing. Being known, or what most would simply call a reputation, is something people gift you over time. It forms through your behaviour and the way you consistently show up for yourself. You don’t have to manufacture it, force it or spend every waking minute trying to manage how you’re perceived by others. A reputation happens naturally as you continue growing into the person you’re becoming. And this is where I think we can run into trouble because the moment we start thinking of ourselves as a brand, our focus can shift. Instead of asking, “Who am I becoming?” we start asking, “How will this look to other people?” The danger is that we start viewing ourselves through the eyes of an audience before we’ve had chance to fully understand ourselves… we start looking at ourselves from the outside in. At first, that might not sound like too much of a problem. In fact, it actually sounds pretty bloody sensible. If you’re running a business, surely you should care about how people feel when they see you. But I don’t believe growth and perception always want the same thing. The thing about growth is that it can look a bit messy from the outside. You change your mind, let go of old ideas and, more often than we’d like to admit, realise you got something wrong. That’s all part of the process. And brand logic doesn’t particularly reward that kind of thinking. Brands gain strength through their consistency. They keep showing up in roughly the same way until people know exactly what to expect from them. And I think that’s where a lot of people can run into a bit of an issue. The more successful a personal brand becomes, the more pressure there can be to keep being the person your audience already knows. To keep talking about the same things, showing up in the same way and feeding the machine that made people pay attention in the first place. That’s the personal brand trap. The human becomes responsible for holding onto a version of themselves they may have already outgrown. And as we see more people choosing freelance careers, building solo businesses and creating opportunities for themselves online, I think this becomes an increasingly important conversation to navigate. I know that perception matters, visibility matters, being known matters, and creating opportunity matters… but so does growth as a human being. Perhaps the challenge isn’t figuring out how to turn people into brands… instead it’s figuring out how to help people become known without trapping them. I’d hate to think that personal branding, the very thing so many people turn to in search of more opportunity, could end up becoming the thing that stops them from becoming who they’re supposed to be. So if I can leave you with a little bit of advice here it would be this: focus on the things you want to be known for, but don’t lose sight of the person you’re becoming along the way. Maybe the goal isn’t to manage perception at all. Perhaps it’s simply to become someone worth paying attention to. Humans are supposed to evolve. Brands are supposed to repeat. The problems arise when we start applying the rules of one to the other, so don’t flatten yourself into a product mindset just because the internet tells you that’s the secret to success. Focus on becoming known for your craft, your kindness and your character. Keep sharing what matters to you because opportunity has a funny way of finding people who do. Just please remember to sprinkle a little patience on yourself along the way. Your mate, James Thoughts on this? Comment below team. I’m excited to hear what you think.
